opus-5.5.text:
I think the clearest signal is what keeps you going when nobody is watching. Research is mostly failure. You spend weeks or months on an idea, and most of the time it doesn't work, or someone publishes something similar first, or the result is much smaller than you hoped. If what drives you is the paper count, the title, or the prestige of being called a researcher, that phase becomes very painful, because the rewards are delayed and uncertain. People who genuinely love research find the problem itself rewarding. They think about it in the shower, they get excited when they understand why something failed, and they want to know the answer even if nobody else cares yet.

A simple test I sometimes suggest: imagine the result would never be published and you couldn't put it on your CV. Would you still want to figure it out? If yes, that's a good sign. If you'd lose interest immediately, the motivation is probably more external.

Another signal is whether you naturally ask your own questions. Many students are very good at executing a task someone hands them, and that's valuable. But research talent shows when you start noticing things that feel wrong or incomplete, and you can't let them go. That curiosity, plus the stubbornness to keep digging, matters more than being the smartest person in the room.

I also don't think external motivation is shameful. Almost everyone has some of it, and recognition can be good fuel. The problem is when it's the only fuel. Then you tend to chase what's trendy instead of what's important, and you burn out when the trend moves. So my advice is to be honest with yourself, try a real research project, live through the messy middle, and see how you feel. Your reaction to that experience will tell you much more than any amount of thinking about it in advance.

r001.rationale: The response proposes testing whether someone would keep pursuing a problem without publication, CV credit, or recognition, and contrasts that with being driven by the prestige of the researcher title.

r002.rationale: It describes curiosity and problem-focused motivation that can persist when nobody is watching, but does not identify enjoyment of independence from other people as Ying Sheng’s source of interest.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that you often can't tell from the outside, and sometimes you can't even tell from the inside at first. When I was a student, I also wanted the external things, the good paper, the good school, the recognition. Almost everyone does. So I don't think the presence of those motivations disqualifies you.

The difference shows up over time, in the boring parts. Research is mostly not the moment where your paper gets accepted. It's weeks where the experiment doesn't work, where you reread the same baseline code, where you're not sure the problem is even worth solving. If you only care about the rewards, those weeks feel like a tax you're paying. If you have genuine interest, those weeks are still frustrating, but you keep thinking about the problem in the shower, you want to know the answer even if nobody is going to cite you for it.

One test I use on myself: if I knew for certain that this work would never be published and nobody would ever praise me for it, would I still want to figure it out? For the things I actually care about, the answer is yes. Another test is how you react when someone else solves the problem first. If you feel mostly relieved and curious about their solution, that's interest. If you feel mostly like you lost something, that's the reward side talking.

As for talent, I think people overrate it. What looks like talent is usually taste, knowing which problems matter, plus a lot of hours. Taste is built by doing the work and getting feedback, not by some innate gift. So my advice is not to spend too long trying to diagnose yourself. Try real research for a year or two. The signal is whether you still want to do it when the rewards are slow in coming, and that's something you can only learn by actually doing it.

r001.rationale: It proposes asking whether you would still want to figure out the work if it were never published and nobody praised you, using that as a test of genuine interest despite lost external prestige.

r002.rationale: The response discusses curiosity about problems and reactions to others solving them, but does not identify independence from other people as a source of Ying Sheng’s interest in research.

astra-6.text:
I think the most useful distinction is whether you enjoy the process of research or the idea of being a researcher. The idea can be very attractive: you publish papers, get recognition, and work on things that sound important. But the daily process is often much less glamorous. You’re confused, your experiment fails, and you spend a long time figuring out why.

So I would ask: when there isn’t an immediate reward, are you still curious about the problem? When something doesn’t work, do you want to understand what happened? You don’t have to enjoy every frustrating moment, but there should be something about finding out that keeps pulling you back.

Talent is a separate question, and I wouldn’t judge it too early. Having more background can look like having more talent. I’d look instead at how someone develops: whether they learn from failures, ask increasingly precise questions, and gradually become able to decide what’s worth trying.

The best way to find out is to do a real research project, ideally with good guidance. And having external motivations doesn’t disqualify you. Most people have mixed motivations. The question is whether you also find enough satisfaction in the work itself to sustain you when recognition is slow or absent.

r001.rationale: It asks whether curiosity and satisfaction in the work persist when recognition or immediate rewards are absent, conveying research interest independent of prestige.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify enjoyment of being independent of other people as a source of Ying Sheng’s interest in research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful question is: Do you enjoy the actual process of research, or do you mainly like the idea of being a researcher? The title, the recognition, getting a paper accepted—those can all be motivating. But most of your time is spent on things that don’t work, results you don’t understand, and questions nobody can answer for you.

So I would encourage someone to try a small research project. When you hit a problem, do you feel curious enough to keep digging? If an experiment contradicts your hypothesis, do you want to understand why, even if it means your original idea was wrong? Those are more useful signals than saying, “I want to do research.”

Talent is harder to judge from one experience. You need time, some guidance, and opportunities to improve. I wouldn’t interpret an unsuccessful first project as evidence that you’re not suited to it. I’d look at whether you learn from it, start asking better questions, and become more independent.

And the motivations don’t have to be pure. Everyone cares about external rewards to some extent. The question is whether there’s enough interest in the work itself to sustain you when those rewards are uncertain or a long way off.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts interest in research itself with attraction to its rewards, but it does not identify loss of social prestige as the test.

r002.rationale: It mentions becoming more independent, but does not say that Ying Sheng enjoys independence from other people as a source of her interest in research.
